definition: Automated optical inspection (AOI) is an automated visual inspection of printed circuit board (PCB) (or LCD, transistor) manufacture where a camera autonomously scans the device under test for both catastrophic failure (e.g.
details: missing component) and quality defects (e.g. fillet size or shape or component skew). It is commonly used in the manufacturing process because it is a non-contact test method. Modern AOI systems increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence and deep learning techniques to improve defect detection and analysis of electronic assemblies. It is implemented at many stages through the manufacturing process including bare board inspection, solder paste inspection (SPI), pre-reflow and post-re-flow as well as other stages. Historically, the primary place for AOI systems has been after solder re-flow or "post-production." This is mainly because post-re-flow AOI systems can inspect for most types of defects (component placement, solder shorts, missing solder, etc.) at one place in the line with one single system. In this way, the faulty boards are reworked and the other boards are sent to the next process stage.

explainer.lead: Automated optical inspection (AOI) uses cameras to check manufactured electronic devices without touching them. It catches missing parts, placement errors, soldering problems, and other defects so faulty boards can be reworked before moving on.

tiers.eli5: AOI is like a very careful robot using its eyes to check something being built. A camera looks over a circuit board and spots problems such as a missing part or crooked placement. Finding those problems early lets workers fix the board instead of sending it farther along with a fault.
tiers.practitioner: AOI is deployed at several manufacturing stages, including bare-board inspection, solder-paste inspection, pre-reflow, and post-reflow. Post-reflow is historically common because one station can check component placement, solder shorts, missing solder, and other defects before routing boards to rework or the next stage. Modern systems increasingly use AI and deep learning for defect detection and analysis.
tiers.paperLevel: AOI is automated visual inspection in which a camera autonomously scans a device under test for catastrophic failures and quality defects. It is a non-contact test method applied to PCB, LCD, and transistor manufacture. Modern implementations increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence and deep learning for defect detection and analysis.

explainer.example: After solder reflow, an AOI camera scans a PCB and finds one missing component, a solder short, and acceptable placement elsewhere. That board is sent for rework, while a board without detected defects continues to the next process stage.

usedIn.name: PCB manufacturing
usedIn.detail: Checks bare boards, solder paste, and assemblies before and after reflow.

usedIn.name: LCD manufacturing
usedIn.detail: Uses automated camera-based visual inspection during manufacture.

usedIn.name: Transistor manufacturing
usedIn.detail: Applies non-contact visual checks to devices under test.

explainer.intuition: A camera takes over the repetitive job of visually checking every device. Because the inspection is non-contact, it can fit into manufacturing without physically probing the board.
howItWorks: Place the board or other device under test in the inspection process.
Let a camera autonomously scan its visible features.
Detect catastrophic failures such as a missing component and quality defects such as component skew or incorrect fillet size or shape.
At a post-reflow station, inspect placement and soldering defects in one pass.
Send faulty boards to rework and pass the others to the next manufacturing stage.
explainer.whyItMatters: AOI brings repeatable, non-contact visual checks to multiple points in electronics manufacturing. A single post-reflow system can catch many defect types, helping separate boards that need rework from those ready to proceed.
misconceptions: AOI is not limited to finished boards: it can inspect bare boards, solder paste, and assemblies before or after reflow.
AOI is not only for catastrophic failures; it also checks quality details such as fillet size or shape and component skew.
AI is an increasingly common enhancement, not a requirement in the basic definition of AOI.
